passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of David” (verse 1). The psalm opens with a question to God: “O LORD, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?” (verse 1).

The answer is a portrait of a person. “He who walks with integrity and practices righteousness, who speaks the truth from his heart” (verse 2). He “has no slander on his tongue” and “does no harm to his neighbor” (verse 3). He “does not revise a costly oath” (verse 4): he keeps his word even when it hurts. He “lends his money without interest and refuses a bribe against the innocent” (verse 5).

It ends with a promise: “He who does these things will never be shaken” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers would picture a worshipper coming up to God's dwelling. ‘Your tent’ recalls the tent David set up for the ark of the covenant in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:17). The ‘holy mountain’ is Zion. Many scholars call Psalm 15 and Psalm 24, which asks almost the same question, ‘entrance psalms’: words spoken as worshippers came up to God's house.

To ‘abide’ is to stay as a guest. The question is: what kind of guest fits God's house?

Look at the list. Almost every line is about a neighbour: speech, harm, money, courts. Lending without interest comes from the law of Moses: “If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest” (Exodus 22:25). In a farming village, a loan was usually help after a bad harvest. Interest could push a poor family into losing its land.
passages.later:
Isaiah asks the same question in fear: “Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire?” He answers with a similar portrait: “He who walks righteously and speaks with sincerity” (Isaiah 33:14-15). Micah sums it up: “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).

Jesus asked for the same kind of life, and more: “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’” (Matthew 5:37). When the tax collector Zacchaeus met Jesus, his money changed hands toward the poor (Luke 19:8).
passages.hard:
Is this a list of things you must do to earn a place with God? Read alone, it can sound that way. But the psalm was given to a people God had already rescued from Egypt and taken as his own. It describes what a guest of God looks like, not how a stranger buys a ticket in.

The rest of the Bible says the same. Psalm 51 shows a man who failed this list badly and was still received with mercy. The New Testament says that no one comes in by their own record: “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2:8). It also says we may now “enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). Then it adds that God's people are “created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (Ephesians 2:10). Grace opens the door. The life in Psalm 15 is what grows in the house.
passages.asks:
Read the list slowly and ask which line is hardest for you. Is it your tongue, a promise that has become costly, or how you treat someone who owes you money?

The psalm does not ask you to be impressive. It asks you to be trustworthy. Pray it as a request: make me this kind of guest in your house.
